svg.aria-label: Diagram: An AWS FIS experiment template contains actions, targets and stop conditions, and AWS FIS carries out real actions on real AWS resources. The stop condition is the only one of the three whose job is to limit harm, and it is a CloudWatch alarm you define rather than a built-in control. Declining to have one is a documented first-class value written as stopConditions with source set to none, so a template with no guardrail is valid and nothing rejects it. When a stop condition fires, FIS stops the experiment and the experiment cannot be resumed, but stopping ends the fault injection rather than reversing what it already did, so instances already terminated stay terminated. Targets are resolved once: FIS identifies all targets at the start of the experiment before any action begins, holds that set for the whole experiment, and fails if no targets are found. Three selection modes scope the set. ALL runs the action on all targets. COUNT of n runs it on that many targets chosen at random. PERCENT of n runs it on that percentage chosen at random, rounding down, so five instances at fifty percent gives two, and four instances at five percent selects no instance at all, in which case the experiment fails rather than running on nothing. If multiple target definitions use the same resource type, FIS can select the same resource more than once, so two actions can land on one instance. Every FIS quota is non-adjustable: five stop conditions and twenty actions per template, which is four actions per guardrail, ten parallel actions per experiment, five active experiments, five hundred templates, a twelve-hour ceiling on an experiment or a single action which is 720 billable action-minutes, and 120-day retention of completed experiment data. Per-action target caps differ by how destructive the action is: 300 instances for terminate, 600 for reboot, and 1,000 pods for pod delete. Billing is per minute an action runs, from start to finish, multiplied by the number of target accounts. The closing rule is to record which alarms were armed next to every experiment result, because completed without an alarm means nothing until you know what the alarm was watching.
svg.title: A stop condition halts the experiment, not the damage
svg.text: The guardrail is a CloudWatch alarm you wrote. Having none is a documented value.
“AWS FIS carries out real actions on real AWS resources in your system.”
WHEN IT FIRES
“AWS FIS stops the experiment. You cannot
resume a stopped experiment.”
Stopping ends the injection. It does not
undo it — terminated stays terminated.
WHEN THERE ISN’T ONE
"stopConditions": [ { "source": "none" } ]
A valid, documented template. Nothing
rejects it, and a completed run looks the
same as one whose alarm never tripped.
Targets are resolved once, at the start, and held for the whole experiment
“AWS FIS identifies all targets at the start … If no targets are found, the experiment fails.”
ALL every target the query matched
COUNT(n) n targets, “chosen … at random” — two runs are not one experiment
PERCENT(n) rounds down; 4 instances at 5% selects none, and the experiment fails
And one resource can be hit twice
“If you define multiple targets using the same target resource type, AWS FIS can select the same resource multiple times.”
Every FIS quota is non-adjustable
stop conditions / template 5 against 20 actions — four actions per guardrail
parallel actions 10 active experiments 5, templates 500
experiment / action ceiling 12 h = 720 billable action-minutes per account
completed data retention 120 d export it, or lose last quarter
Target caps scale with damage: 300 terminate, 600 reboot, 1,000 pod-delete. Billed per action-minute per target account.
Record which alarms were armed, next to every experiment result.
“Completed, no alarm tripped” is two findings: the application held, or the alarm watched the wrong signal. The
distinction lives in the template, never in the result.
FIS supplies the mechanism that stops. You supply the judgement about when — and that is the half that decides
whether a green experiment report is evidence or a completion record.
